title: Book IV: Three Love Problems — Chapter XLI
paragraphs:
By swaggering could I never thrive,
For the rain it raineth every day.
—_Twelfth Night_.
The dealings Caleb Garth had mentioned between Mr. Bulstrode and Mr. Joshua Rigg Featherstone over the land belonging to Stone Court had led the two men to exchange a letter or two.

Who can say what writing may bring about? Words carved in stone may lie face down for centuries on a deserted beach, or “rest quietly under the drums and tramplings of many conquests,” and finally reveal the secrets of stolen power and other scandals that were gossip in long-vanished empires. The world seems to be one enormous whispering gallery. Our little lifetimes often reproduce these circumstances in miniature. A stone kicked about by generations of country fools may, through a curious chain of small events, come to a scholar’s notice. His work may eventually make it the means of dating invasions and unlocking the mysteries of religions. In the same way, a scrap of ink-covered paper, long used innocently as wrapping or to plug a gap, may at last unfold before the one pair of eyes whose knowledge can turn it into the beginning of a catastrophe. To Uriel, watching the history of the planets from the sun, either result would be equally coincidental.

After that rather elevated comparison, I feel less embarrassed about drawing attention to low people. However little we like their interference, they do a great deal to determine the world’s course. Certainly it would be good if we could reduce their numbers; perhaps we might do something by being less careless about bringing them into existence. In social terms, most people would have called Joshua Rigg unnecessary. But people like Peter Featherstone, whom nobody ever asked to reproduce themselves, are the very last to wait for a request, in prose or verse. In this instance the copy took more of its outward appearance from the mother. In a woman, frog-like features, combined with rosy cheeks and a rounded figure, can have considerable charm for certain admirers. The result is sometimes a frog-faced man, surely desirable to no class of intelligent beings. Especially when he suddenly appears to defeat other people’s expectations—the worst possible way for a socially unnecessary person to present himself.

Yet Mr. Rigg Featherstone’s low qualities were entirely of the sober, water-drinking sort. From morning until night he was as sleek, tidy and cool as the frog he resembled. Old Peter had secretly chuckled over a son almost more calculating than himself and far harder to disturb. I should add that he looked after his fingernails meticulously, and intended to marry a well-educated young woman, not yet selected, who was good-looking and had indisputably respectable middle-class connections. His nails and his modest ambitions thus compared well with those of most gentlemen, although his ambitions had been shaped only by his opportunities as a clerk and accountant in the smaller businesses of a port town. He thought the country Featherstones absurdly simple people. For their part, they considered his upbringing in a seaport a further aggravation of the monstrous fact that their brother Peter—and, still more, Peter’s property—should have such connections.

Seen from the two windows of Stone Court’s panelled sitting room, the garden and gravel drive had never looked neater. Mr. Rigg Featherstone stood gazing out at them with his hands behind his back, their owner now. It was uncertain, though, whether he wanted to contemplate his grounds or merely turn his back on the person standing in the middle of the room, legs wide apart and hands in his trouser pockets. In every respect this visitor contrasted with the sleek, cool Rigg. Plainly approaching sixty, he was red-faced and hairy, with plenty of grey in his bushy whiskers and thick curls. His rather stout body made the worn seams of his clothes more conspicuous. He had the manner of a swaggering man determined to attract attention even at a fireworks display, convinced that his comments on someone else’s performance would interest people more than the performance itself.

His name was John Raffles. He sometimes jokingly added W.A.G. to his signature, explaining that he had once been taught by Leonard Lamb of Finsbury, who put B.A. after his name. It was he, Raffles, who had thought up the joke of calling that celebrated headmaster Ba-Lamb. Such were Mr. Raffles’s looks and turn of mind. Both seemed to carry the stale smell of the commercial travellers’ rooms in the hotels of that time.
“Come along, Josh,” he was saying in a deep, rumbling voice. “Think of it this way: your poor mother’s getting on in years, and now you could afford to give her a decent sum to make her comfortable.”
“Not while you’re alive. She’ll never be comfortable as long as you live,” Rigg answered in his cool, high voice. “Whatever I give her, you’ll take.”

“You’ve got a grudge against me, Josh. I know that. But come on—man to man, no nonsense—a little money to start with could help me make a first-rate business of the shop. The tobacco trade’s growing. I’d be cutting off my nose to spite my face if I didn’t make the most of it. For my own sake, I’d stick to it like a flea to a fleece. I’d always be there. And nothing would please your poor mother more. I’ve about finished sowing my wild oats—I’m past fifty-five. I want to settle down by my own fireside. Once I put my back into the tobacco business, I could bring brains and experience to it that you wouldn’t easily find anywhere else. I don’t want to keep troubling you. I want to get everything on the right track once and for all. Think about it, Josh—man to man—and think of your poor mother, comfortable for the rest of her life. I’ve always been fond of the old woman, by Jove!”
“Finished?” Mr. Rigg asked quietly, still facing the window.
“Yes, _I’ve_ finished,” said Raffles. He took hold of his hat on the table before him and pushed it forward as though concluding a speech.

“Then listen. The more often you say something, the less I’ll believe it. The more you want me to do something, the stronger my reason never to do it. Do you imagine I’ll forget how you kicked me when I was a boy, and took all the best food from me and my mother? Do you think I’ve forgotten how you kept coming home, selling everything, pocketing the money and leaving us helpless again? I’d be glad to see you whipped behind a cart. My mother was a fool where you were concerned. She had no right to give me a stepfather, and she’s paid for it. She’ll get her weekly allowance, and nothing more. And even that will stop if you dare set foot on this property again, or follow me into this part of the country. Next time you come through those gates, the dogs and the wagon driver’s whip will drive you out.”

At these last words, Rigg turned and fixed his bulging, icy eyes on Raffles. The contrast between them was as sharp as it could have been eighteen years earlier, when Rigg was an unappealing boy who invited a kick and Raffles the rather stocky Adonis of bars and back rooms. But Rigg now had the advantage. Anyone overhearing them might have expected Raffles to slink away like a beaten dog. Nothing of the sort. He made the face he habitually made when he lost at a game, then relaxed into a laugh and pulled a brandy flask from his pocket.
“Come on, Josh,” he coaxed. “Give me a drop of brandy and a sovereign for the journey home, and I’ll be off. On my honour! I’ll go like a bullet, _by_ Jove!”

“Understand this,” said Rigg, taking out a bunch of keys. “If I see you again, I won’t speak to you. I acknowledge no more connection with you than with a crow. And if you claim a connection with me, all you’ll gain is a reputation for what you are—a spiteful, brazen, bullying scoundrel.”

“Well, that’s a pity, Josh,” said Raffles, pretending to scratch his head and raise his brows in bewilderment. “I’m very fond of you. _By_ Jove, I am! I like nothing better than tormenting you—you’re so like your mother—and now I must give it up. But we have a bargain about the brandy and the sovereign.”

He thrust the flask forward, and Rigg took his keys to a fine old oak bureau. The movement had reminded Raffles that the flask was dangerously loose in its leather case. He noticed a folded paper lying inside the fireplace guard, picked it up and pushed it under the leather to hold the glass firmly in place.

By then Rigg had returned with a brandy bottle. He filled the flask and handed over a sovereign, without either looking at Raffles or speaking. After locking the bureau again, he went back to the window and stared out as expressionlessly as at the beginning of the visit. Meanwhile Raffles took a little drink, screwed the flask shut and tucked it into his side pocket with deliberately irritating slowness, making a face behind his stepson’s back.
“Farewell, Josh—and if for ever!” Raffles said, looking back as he opened the door.

Rigg watched him cross the grounds and turn into the lane. The grey day had developed into a light drizzle. It freshened the hedges and grassy edges of the side roads, and hurried the labourers loading the last bundles of grain. Raffles walked with the awkward gait of a town loafer forced to travel a stretch of country on foot. Amid the damp countryside’s quiet and industry, he looked as out of place as a baboon escaped from a menagerie. But only calves long past weaning stared at him, and only the little water rats, scurrying away as he approached, showed any dislike of his appearance.

On reaching the main road he had the good luck to be overtaken by a stagecoach, which took him to Brassing. There he boarded the recently built railway, remarking to the other passengers that he thought it had been properly broken in now that it had killed Huskisson. On most occasions Mr. Raffles maintained his sense of having been educated at an academy and of being able, if he chose, to pass muster anywhere. Indeed, he never met a fellow human being whom he did not feel entitled to ridicule and torment, quite sure that everyone else present would enjoy the entertainment.

He performed that role now as cheerfully as if his journey had been a complete success, taking frequent drinks from his flask. The paper wedged around it was a letter signed _Nicholas Bulstrode_. But Raffles was unlikely to disturb it while it was serving its present useful purpose.
